Among the various approaches for controlling the THz waves, the application of external stimuli such as optical pumping and thermal or electric fields is widely employed as a promising strategy for modulation. This review focuses on recent advances in THz modulation based on different materials including 2D semiconductors and metamaterials with attention to their response under external stimuli. In addition, strain-driven THz modulation in non-centrosymmetric piezoelectric materials including organic and semi-organic crystals is examined with an emphasis on their ability to establish strong coupling between propagating THz waves and lattice vibrations under piezoelectric resonance conditions. We further highlight earlier reports on strain-driven THz modulation in lithium niobate (LiNbO3) and critically assess the potential of several other nonlinear optical crystals exhibiting piezoelectric resonance peaks suitable for strain-driven THz modulation. An overview of THz modulators integrated with tunable materials is presented highlighting their operating principles and key performance metrics comprising modulation speed, bandwidth, modulation depth and insertion loss.

items.title: Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models
items.summary: Quantum impurity models, which describe a small but strongly-interacting subsystem coupled to a large noninteracting bath, are the computational core of dynamical mean field theory and play an important role in simulating strongly correlated materials. We develop quantum algorithms for efficiently simulating these models at low temperatures and with high precision. For any impurity model on $n$ fermionic modes with fixed impurity size: (1) We give a quantum algorithm that prepares the thermal state at inverse temperature $β$ to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. This algorithm is the first to achieve both polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and polylogarithmic scaling in the precision. When the Hamiltonian has an inverse-polynomial spectral gap, our quantum algorithm prepares its ground state to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(1/δ))$. (2) We further give a quantum algorithm that prepares a purification of the thermal state in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. Using this purification, we estimate static and dynamical properties with error $δ$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $β$ and linear in $1/δ$ up to polylogarithmic factors, achieving the Heisenberg scaling. Our algorithms build on quantum Gibbs samplers, which are quantum analogues of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. By using global jump operators instead of local ones, we avoid the $\exp(β)$ overhead commonly associated with quantum Gibbs samplers, making them efficient for impurity models even at low temperatures.

items.title: Generation and non-thermal annealing of dislocations and atomic-scale roughness by nonlinear surface acoustic waves
items.summary: Surface acoustic waves (SAWs) are widely used to probe near-surface material properties and microstructure, but their potential to drive permanent structural modification remains largely unexplored. Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations reveal the mechanisms of defect generation and evolution induced by nonlinear Rayleigh waves in Pt. Strong crystallographic dependence of the nonlinear evolution is observed. SAWs on Pt(111) undergo rapid nonlinear sharpening and shock formation, with localized elastic energy and increasing near-surface stresses, whereas much weaker sharpening on Pt(001) allows dissipation to compete effectively with shock formation. For sufficiently strong SAWs on Pt(111), Shockley partial dislocations are emitted from the surface when the resolved shear stress approaches the theoretical shear strength. The highly localized and rapidly changing stress field at the shock front activates multiple slip systems and promotes crossslip and reactions between Shockley partials, producing complex dislocation structures with sessile stair-rod segments. Subsequent SAW interactions activate dislocation sources on slip systems where the stress is insufficient for homogeneous nucleation, leading, in one case, to sequential emission of Shockley partials and formation of a subsurface twinned domain. Repeated SAW passages progressively reduce dislocation density, demonstrating SAW-driven nonthermal annealing. Dislocation interactions with the free surface generate atomic-scale steps, terraces, and other under-coordinated configurations, providing a microscopic pathway for permanent surface modification that may contribute to the acoustically enhanced catalytic activity observed on Pt surfaces. These results establish nonlinear SAWs as drivers of nonthermal defect generation, restructuring, and annealing, opening opportunities for acoustic processing of near-surface microstructure.

items.title: A Unified Energy-Density Framework for Moiré Interface Energetics and Mechanics
items.summary: The mechanical response of moiré interfaces depends on how atomic registry combines with contact size and boundary geometry. An analytical description must retain this discrete lattice information while connecting microscopic interactions to the energetics of finite contacts. Here, we develop a unified energy-density framework for rigid van der Waals interfaces by expressing registry-dependent pair potentials and atomic densities in reciprocal space. The resulting formulation accommodates different lattice bases and atomic species, linking single-atom and molecular adsorption to infinite bilayers and finite crystalline contacts. Explicit expressions for circular and regular polygonal flakes separate the area contribution from boundary-dependent terms and connect microscopic corrugation coefficients to energy barriers, rotational torques, and interlayer shear stiffnesses. The boundary analysis recovers the quarter-power area scaling of the barrier envelope for circular flakes and distinguishes bounded oscillations from square-root area scaling for polygonal contacts according to edge orientation. A dimensionless criterion characterizes the polygon-to-circle crossover in terms of moiré wavelength, flake size, and side number. Direct-summation benchmarks support the finite-domain expressions, while calculations for two-dimensional ice on graphene demonstrate the corresponding boundary-scaling trends in a molecular lattice. Applications to interlayer shear and graphite compression connect the same microscopic interaction description to tangential and normal mechanical responses. The framework establishes an analytical connection between microscopic registry, moiré periodicity, and finite-domain geometry, providing a basis for understanding and tailoring the energetics and mechanics of van der Waals contacts.

items.title: Selective Cr Leaching Mediates Reconstruction of Ultrathin High-Entropy Oxide Nanosheets for Oxygen Evolution
authors: Qiao Xie, Zhen Yuan, Yingjie Yu, Tianyi Zhu, Haijun Zhang, Yuhua Wang, Shaowei Zhang, Wenzhong Lv, and Wen Lei
items.summary: Abstract Two-dimensional high-entropy oxide (2D-HEO) nanosheets are potential candidates for oxygen evolution electrocatalysis (OER), and we report a polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP)-assisted freeze-drying route to prepare spinel (FeCoNiCrMn) 3 O 4 HEO nanosheets for probing element-selective surface reconstruction in alkaline media. Time-resolved characterizations confirm retention of the sheetlike morphology alongside the generation of a porous amorphous surface layer induced by preferential near-surface Cr dissolution. Theoretical calculations designate Cr as the most vacancy susceptible cation in the spinel lattice. Cr vacancies activate O 2p states and reorganize adjacent metal 3d orbitals, redistributing adsorbate–surface interactions for the OER. This work identifies selective cation leaching as an intrinsic trigger for adaptive active-interface reconstruction and provides a mechanistic understanding of interface dynamics in multicomponent high-entropy electrocatalysts.

items.title: Coupled H + /Na + Interlayer Regulation and Porous Nanoflower Architecture Enable Superior Zinc-Ion Storage in Hydrogen Sodium Vanadate Cathodes
authors: Xingyuan Wu, Yan Yan, Jiangshan Liu, Jiliang Liu, Kun Rui, Huijuan Lin, Jixin Zhu, and Wei Huang
items.summary: Abstract The commercialization of aqueous zinc-ion batteries is critically hindered by slow ion transport and progressive structural degradation of cathodes. Preintercalation of foreign species offers an effective strategy to address these limitations. Herein, H + /Na + cointercalated hydrogen sodium vanadate (HNaV 6 O 16 ·4H 2 O, denoted as HNVO-5) is synthesized via a facile and rapid one-step hydrothermal route at 140 °C for 5 h. The hierarchical nanoflower morphology provides interconnected pores, abundant accessible active sites, and shortened Zn 2+ transport pathways. Besides, the inserted Na + ions serve as interlayer pillars for stabilizing the layered V–O framework, while the H + ions provide local charge compensation that mitigates the electrostatic interaction between Zn 2+ and the host framework, thereby lowering the diffusion barrier. Consequently, the optimized cathode exhibits excellent electrochemical performance in both coin cell and flexible pouch cell. This work validates a practical strategy for the rapid synthesis of dual-ion cointercalated cathodes for aqueous zinc-ion batteries with enhanced performance.

items.title: Silicon Nanowire Photoconductors in Electronic Shuttering Mode for Light Detection at a Telecommunication Wavelength
authors: Yinchu Shen, Huayou Liu, Jinyuan Chen, Kevin Jin, Kenneth B. Crozier, and Yaping Dan
items.summary: Abstract Silicon photodetectors at 1550 nm are desirable for integrated photonics but face weak sub-bandgap absorption. We report a monolithic silicon nanowire photoconductor driven by Er/O/B codoped PN junctions and operated with an integrated electronic shutter. A junction photovoltage modulates the nanowire conducting cross-section, while an NMOS switch periodically resets the junction under continuous illumination. The fitted low-irradiance responsivity limit is 1.86 A/W, approximately 4 orders of magnitude above that of the driving diode alone. The measured electronic-shuttering bandwidth is approximately 8 kHz. Dark-noise-based limiting estimates give a minimum noise-equivalent power of approximately 10 –12 W/√Hz and a maximum specific detectivity of approximately 2 × 10 10 Jones near 5 kHz; finite-irradiance performance uses the corresponding illuminated noise. Single-pixel imaging under continuous 1550 nm illumination and gate-synchronized detection demonstrates spatial reconstruction. This architecture combines sub-bandgap detection, current amplification, and electrical modulation on silicon.

items.title: A Supra-amphiphilic DNA Complex for Delivering Mechanosensitive Gold Nanoclusters into Lipid Membranes
authors: Yan Zhou, Tonglu Lu, Siyuan Zhang, Yang Yang, Hui Lu, Gaoang Zhou, Jianxin Yang, Jinghuang Chen, Haoran Zheng, Mulin Duan, Mingqiang Li, Xiaoliang Chen, and Jianlei Shen
items.summary: Abstract The delivery of hydrophobic, nonplanar mechanosensitive probes into lipid bilayers is a prerequisite for interrogating membrane biophysics, yet it remains challenging due to limited delivery strategies. Here, we report a supra-amphiphilic DNA complex that dynamically assembles a hydrophobic Au 8 nanocluster (Au 8 -TPA) with amphiphilic single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), rendering the nanocluster water-dispersible without chemical modification and enabling its efficient insertion into lipid bilayers. All-atom molecular dynamics simulations reveal a three-step “anchor-reorient-insert” mechanism driven by synergistic electrostatic and van der Waals interactions in which the ssDNA anchors to the membrane surface and guides the nanocluster into a vertical insertion configuration. Once embedded, the Au 8 -TPA probe reports membrane tension through intramolecular restriction-induced fluorescence-to-phosphorescence transition, exhibiting a 17.1-fold variation in phosphorescence lifetime under osmotic shock in model lipid vesicles. This work establishes a versatile platform for delivering membrane-impermeable functional nanomaterials into lipid bilayers and provides a noncanonical mechanosensitive probing strategy for interrogating membrane biophysics.

items.title: Projecting Fermions into Exact Scar Towers: Local Protection across Phase Transitions
items.summary: We construct exact scar towers in $SO(n)$ ($n\ge3$) spin chains by Gutzwiller projection of $n$-flavor flat-band Kitaev chains. The projected roots have only singlet and antisymmetric components on each bond. These local constraints allow a staggered flavor flip to generate an equidistant tower. The root and its first descendant exhaust the two-site configurations that are visited by the tower, leaving an orthogonal bond subspace unvisited. Deformations within this subspace can break $SO(n)$ symmetry and reshape the low-energy physics without altering the exact scar tower. A polarization-selective deformation drives an exact first-order transition from the symmetry-protected topological phase to a ferromagnetic phase. The tower retains its wave functions and absolute energies across the phase transition, including at the gapless point. Exact scars therefore need not inherit the symmetries, order parameters, or criticality of the ground state.

items.title: Fracton Topological Holography
items.summary: Topological Holography (TH) is a framework of representing $(d-1)$-dimensional quantum systems with a $d$-dimensional sandwich, consisting of a topological order bulk, a gapped top boundary and a dynamical bottom boundary. Dualities and non-invertible symmetries are represented by the change of top boundary in the TH framework. Existing studies have focused on sandwiches with liquid topological bulk, in this paper we examine some fracton bulks, where we call the framework Fracton Topological Holography (FTH). In particular, the X-cube FTH induces the transverse field plaquette Ising model (TFPIM) version Kramers--Wannier duality, the duality between TFPIM and the two-dimensional $90^\circ$ quantum compass model, and the self-duality of quantum compass model. Haah's code FTH induces a duality of transverse-field generalized Ising models (TFGIMs). The two examples illustrate at least a part of type-I fracton (X-cube) and a part of type-II fracton (Haah's code) models can be used to construct FTH sandwiches. Moreover, we construct an explicit Sequential Quantum Circuit (SQC) switching the top boundary of X-cube sandwich, realizing the TFPIM version KW duality.

items.title: Indentation-induced polar domain reconfiguration in the charge-density-wave semiconductor EuTe4
items.summary: Controlling polar domains in conducting materials by external fields could unlock polarization-based electronic functionalities, yet remains experimentally challenging. While mechanical actuation driven by local strain, stress, or strain gradients has been proposed as an external-voltage-free route, its experimental demonstration in relatively conducting polar materials remains limited. Here we demonstrate mechanically induced polar-domain reconfiguration in the charge-density-wave (CDW) semiconductor EuTe4 at room temperature, whose resistivity is on the order of 10 m$Ω$cm. Polarized-light microscopy and second-harmonic-generation measurements reveal CDW-induced in-plane polarization domains with an approximately 90 $^\circ$ domain configuration. Local indentation with a $\sim$1 $μ$m-apex-radius needle reconfigures these domains, producing write/erase-like changes in wedge-shaped regions. These results establish local mechanical-field domain engineering in a relatively conducting CDW semiconductor, with possible contributions from both ferroelastic-like and flexoelectric mechanisms.

items.title: Soliton Propagation of Zero Sound in Superfluid $^3$He-B
items.summary: Nonlinear equations for zero sound interacting with the B-phase collective modes are derived by treating $^3$He-B as a medium of two-level ``molecules'' (Cooper pairs), The nonlinear equations reduce to known results from kinetic theory in the linear response limit. Soliton solutions to the nonlinear equations are discussed in context with the experiments of Polturak et al.

items.title: Characterizing electronic scattering rates with transport in multiterminal devices
items.summary: Strongly interacting electrons in clean two-dimensional devices are theorized to exhibit many distinct transport regimes, such as ballistic, hydrodynamic, or diffusive. Realistic samples often lie in crossover regimes between these idealized limits. We show how a single experiment on a multiterminal device can distinguish these regimes and constrain the relevant scattering rates without space-resolved imaging. Using a linearized Boltzmann model in a five-terminal geometry, we find that current partition among the drain contacts diagnoses the ballistic-hydrodynamic-Ohmic crossover and allows extraction of momentum-relaxing and momentum-conserving scattering rates in the crossover regime. The same geometry also exhibits clear signatures of the tomographic regime, potentially allowing for a quantitative discrimination between viscous and tomographic flow in experiments. Our results demonstrate that multiterminal devices are a simpler experimental route to characterize transport regimes in electron liquids, relative to space-resolved imaging experiments.

items.title: Valence band, electron correlation, and possible temperature dependent change in the electronic structure near $E_F$ of a candidate of ambient-pressure nickelate superconductors Sr$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$Cl$_2$
items.summary: Photoemission spectroscopy (PES) studies of Sr$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$Cl$_2$ (Sr3252), a candidate ambient-pressure bilayer nickelate superconductor, have been performed to investigate the electronic structure. Valence band spectra, which are compared with DFT and DFT+U calculations, reveal dominant Ni 3$d$ $t_{2g}$-derived states located around 0.6 eV binding energy with a shoulder around 0.2 eV that can be attributed to states with a dominant Ni 3$d_{3z2-r2}$ character. The overall valence band shape is better reproduced by the simulated spectrum of DFT+U (= 3 eV), providing an experimental estimation of the strength of electron correlation. High-resolution PES near the Fermi level ($E_F$) exhibits marked temperature dependence, which cannot be fully understood by a broadening due to coupling of a photo-hole to phonons alone and suggests change in electronic structure. The results provide fundamental electronic structure information of Sr3252, which is useful to further explore the superconductivity of Sr3252.

items.title: NEP-Spin: A spin-dependent neuroevolution potential for large-scale spin--lattice simulations
items.summary: NEP-Spin is a \glsentrylong{nep} for coupled atomic motion and variable-length magnetic moments. Local bond and spin tensors give an energy invariant under independent spin and spatial rotations without \glsentrylong{soc} and under joint rotations with it. We benchmark energies, atomic forces, and magnetic forces on public datasets for collinear Fe--Al and noncollinear Fe. In multiferroic \glsentrylong{bfo}, the predicted zero-field cycloid period is 69.7~nm, compared with 62--63~nm from neutron scattering. An electric field of 20~mV/Å opposite to the polarization lengthens the period to 93.2~nm, while imposing the same polar displacement at zero field gives 85.1~nm. In a uniform antiferromagnetic cell at fixed lattice vectors, 6~T magnetic fields along orthogonal basal axes reorient the Fe moments and give opposite signs of the ionic polarization change $ΔP_y$. First-principles ionic relaxations at the predicted moment vectors reproduce both signs. In a 2.79-million-atom ferroelectric twin, the cycloid rotation planes tilt by different amounts from their shared initial plane and remain distinct over 10~ps at 100~K. At 10~ps the propagation axes lie within about $7^\circ$ of their initial directions. With inertial spin dynamics, GPUMD advances a 5.93-million-atom BiFeO$_3$ cell at 21.8 million atom-steps per second on four RTX 4090 GPUs.

items.title: Stable but Hidden: Identifiability and Experimental Design under Missing Compositional Support
items.summary: AI-guided scientific discovery often uses inexpensive predictors to allocate scarce verification measurements. We study a structural failure when relevant components have been observed separately but never jointly: distinct admissible response functions can agree on all observed compositions while disagreeing on the missing combinations. Additional same-support data cannot resolve this ambiguity, and agreement among fitted models need not expose it. We characterize the unresolved directions as an invisible subspace $\mathcal{N}_T(\mathcal{F}) = \ker \mathcal{R}_T$, whose geometry determines oracle zero-shot ambiguity and minimax risk under a symmetric, bounded ambiguity class. When the missing response lies in an $r$-dimensional, well-conditioned linear basis, optimally designed joint measurements achieve minimax integrated risk $Θ(σ^2 r/m)$, with classical $I$-optimality the fixed-design criterion. We validate on materials. In electrocatalysis, a six-dimensional support-derived structural basis (a prior on candidate directions, not an identified physical model) reduces held-out MSE against a dimension-matched generic basis (median paired ratio 0.75, improving 98% of 60 element pairs at $m = 15$), while $I$-optimal and same-basis posterior-variance acquisition show no detected difference. In Materials Project, removing joint property labels reduces $E_{\text{above hull}}$ ranking on 90% of 30 element pairs, more than matched data-removal controls, under a frozen pretrained representation. Pair difficulty is reproducible across learners but poorly predicted by zero-label ensemble disagreement; 20 joint measurements enable transferable pair-level rankings without reliable absolute calibration. In practice, experiment selection should ask which relationships the observed support leaves unidentified before asking where a fitted model is least certain.

items.title: Reconstructing Pure-State OTOCs from Forward-Time Linear Response
items.summary: We show that the connected out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC) of any pure state can be reconstructed exactly from commutator linear responses alone. The protocol requires no time reversal, no ancilla, no double copy, and no weak measurement: a unitary string pulse, forward many-body evolution, and a single local readout suffice. An average over a complete basis of pulse generators yields the OTOC exactly. We further show that the measurement can be made sparse by restricting the pulses to a fixed operator weight, which turns the truncation into an analytically controlled spectral filter: the deterministic bias can be computed before the experiment and cleanly separated from the statistical sampling variance. For Gaussian states, the finite-weight response is exactly proportional to the full OTOC after a known combinatorial rescaling. For quantum chaotic systems, the typical residual is suppressed as a power law in the sector size. Exact-diagonalization benchmarks in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and a nonintegrable Ising chain confirm these predictions.

items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery
items.summary: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.

items.title: P-adic numbers and kernels
items.summary: We discuss the relation between p-adic numbers and kernels in view of a recent large deviation theory for mean-field spin glasses. As an application we show several fundamental properties of numerical bases in kernel language. In particular, we show that the Derrida's Generalized Random Energy Model can be interpreted as a (random) numerical base. We also show an application to the Primon gas and the Riemann Zeta Function by constructing a kernel representation of the Primon gas based on a finite p-base, thereby establishing a concrete link between number theory and kernel theory.

items.title: Classification of Thouless pumps with non-invertible symmetries and implications for Floquet phases
items.summary: We study symmetry preserving adiabatic and Floquet dynamics of one-dimensional systems. Using quasiadiabatic evolution, we establish a correspondence between adiabatic cycles and invertible defects generated by spatially truncated Thouless pump operators. Employing the classification of gapped phases by module categories, we show that the Thouless pumps are classified by the group of autoequivalences of the module category. We then explicitly construct Thouless pump operators for minimal lattice models with $\text{Vec}_G$, Rep($G$), and Rep($H$) symmetries, and show how the Thouless pump operators have the group structure of autoequivalences. The Thouless pump operators, together with Hamiltonians with gapped ground states, are then used to construct Floquet drives. An analytic solution for the Floquet phase diagram characterized by winding numbers is constructed when the Floquet drives obey an Onsager algebra. Our approach points the way to a general connection between distinct Thouless pumps and distinct families of Floquet phases.

items.title: Solids activated by multi-body nonreciprocity
items.summary: Field-mediated forces between particles can be both nonreciprocal and irreducibly multi-body, giving rise to emergent activity in systems of individually passive particles. While prior work extensively studied how multi-body nonreciprocity can activate few-body systems, fuel intermittency, and drive liquid-like behavior, the effect on the solid state of large particle ensembles is less explored. Here we use two-dimensional, close-packed rafts of identical, athermal, acoustically levitated microspheres to show how multi-body nonreciprocity injects activity in solids. At the level of both individual particles and collective dynamics, crystalline rafts exhibit persistent circulations with no net handedness. The rafts also exhibit a phonon-like dispersion relation corresponding to a large Poisson ratio, indicating an induced softness to shear. Within the bulk, lattice symmetry masks microscopic nonreciprocity, although it can manifest in renormalized, reciprocal elastic coefficients. At dislocations and raft edges, where this symmetry is broken, multi-body nonreciprocal interactions act as local generators of activity. A coarse-grained microscopic model of multi-body nonreciprocity, calibrated on three-particle simulations, recovers the rafts' experimentally observed dispersion relations and localized activity. Using these findings, we illustrate how to harness defect-induced activity for programmable movement by arranging microscopic dislocations to drive macroscopic propulsion and rotation of a whole raft.

items.title: Trajectory arclength reveals thermodynamic criticality
items.summary: Thermodynamic criticality arises at continuous phase transitions, where collective interactions produce non-analytic behavior in equilibrium thermodynamic quantities in the thermodynamic limit. We show that this criticality also leaves an analytically predictable signature in the arclength of microscopic Hamiltonian trajectories. For the attractive Hamiltonian mean-field model, we derive the thermodynamic limit of the equilibrium-averaged arclength, formulated as a normalized Lagrangian descriptor, and demonstrate that it develops a kink precisely at the phase transition. We trace this non-analyticity to spontaneous magnetization and derive the leading critical finite-size correction, scaling as $N^{-1/2}$ with an explicit analytical prefactor. Simulations with up to $10^5$ degrees of freedom confirm both predictions without adjustable parameters. Requiring neither tangent-space evolution nor prior specification of an order parameter for its computation, trajectory arclength provides a simple, quantitative link between microscopic Hamiltonian motion and collective thermodynamic criticality.

items.title: The response field approach to path integral control
items.summary: This paper investigates non-linear path integral control problems within the response field formalism of nonequilibrium field theory. The aim of this work is exploratory, based on the identification of correspondences between backward adjoint processes and the response field of non-equilibrium statistical physics, whose properties have not been set out in an optimal control setting. The response field is found to play an analogous role to the backward adjoint process under the stochastic maximum principle. In particular, the gradient of the optimal cost-to-go at the initial time, which is proportional to the optimal control, is given by the average of the response field at the initial time. In contrast to the case of non-equilibrium dynamics, the response function is found to be acausal in the control setting. The linear-quadratic case of path integral control is studied, confirming it as the free theory, meaning that solving the control problem is equivalent to completing the square and determining the propagator for a two point boundary value problem. The developments presented here are a necessary prelude to applications based on field theoretic approximation, for both path integral control and their dual inference problems.

items.title: Domain advantage in two-dimensional quantum-device design with multi-modal agentic harness
items.summary: High-quality two-dimensional quantum devices are commonly fabricated from mechanically exfoliated crystals, whose irregular shapes and placement require a lithographic layout tailored to each specimen. Drawing these layouts remains largely manual. We introduce qlaybench, a benchmark that tests whether language-model agents can turn microscope images and experimental requirements into device layouts that fit the specimen. Agents with conventional tools often construct devices when material outlines are supplied, but struggle to identify those outlines from images. Modelled on the human workflow, qlaybot, a multimodal agentic harness, connects image interpretation to the tools used to align images, draw device features and inspect the resulting layout. We evaluate each layout with checks drawn from practical design experience, asking whether it fits the specimen and connects its intended components. With greater computational effort, an agent using qlaybot passes 81.5% of the benchmark tasks, compared with 24.1% when it uses conventional tools. This domain advantage highlights the importance of connecting scientific interpretation of a specimen to geometric design and provides a route towards reducing manual effort in two-dimensional quantum-device fabrication.

items.title: Geometric Polarization-Virial Theorems for Field-Induced Dipolar Interactions and Force Reversal
items.summary: Electric fields can turn attraction into repulsion between far-separated atoms, yet the complete angular mechanical structure governing this reversal has remained unknown. Here, we uncover an entropy-like geometric structure: the cubically weighted interaction free energy, r^3 F(r), is nondecreasing under physical dilation. This structure unifies two exact polarization-virial theorems for arbitrary stable quasistatic dipole assemblies and fully retarded dipole pairs under stated conditions. Consequently, the free energy has at most one zero and energetic cancellation precedes mechanical cancellation. A force zero retains strictly positive energy, whereas an energy zero retains an attractive force. The resulting analytical angular fine structure is resolved by a quantum harmonic oscillator pair, yielding the complete arbitrary-angle interaction energy and radial force that recover quantum-perturbative results. The conventional dipolar magic angle splits into strictly ordered energy- and force-zero angles; the latter uniquely bounds the radially repulsive sector and carries a positive energy barrier. Derived scaling laws and finite-sphere calculations provide experimentally testable signatures from microscopic dipoles to macroscopic polarizable bodies.

items.title: Lie-Poisson Formulation of Dissipative Spin Hydrodynamics
items.summary: Covariance and the second law cannot fix how fluid flow couples to spin, since reversible couplings produce no entropy. We show that the spin commutation relations and the Poincaré algebra fix these couplings. Reversibly, a flow exerts no torque on the spin: its magnitude per particle is conserved, its direction is Fermi--Walker transported, and spin--shear couplings reflect a deforming triad. The magnitude changes only through higher multipoles, as in spinor condensates, or dissipation, whose first-order spin--shear coupling reorients the spin away from the vorticity above a critical shear rate.

items.title: Nonmonotonic In-Plane Thermal Transport in Metal-Embedded Graphitic Carbon Nitride
items.summary: Embedding metal atoms within the intrinsic cavities of graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) modifies its local bonding and vibrational properties, yet its consequences for lattice thermal transport remain poorly understood. Here, we combine a machine-learned potential (MLP) with homogeneous nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (HNEMD) to investigate in-plane thermal transport in Cu-embedded g-C3N4 across the full range of cavity occupation. The thermal conductivity exhibits a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on Cu occupation, decreasing at intermediate occupation and partially recovering as the cavities approach full occupation. Frequency-resolved analysis reveals that this behavior originates from the competition between two phonon contributions. The low-frequency vibrations introduced by Cu couple to the intrinsic modes of g-C3N4, reconstructing the phonon dispersion and suppressing thermal transport below 10 THz. With increasing Cu occupation, the collective mechanical response of the N atoms surrounding the cavities is enhanced, accompanied by increased phonon group velocities in the 20-30 THz range and a corresponding recovery of the high-frequency thermal contribution. The competition between the saturating low-frequency suppression and the increasing high-frequency contribution gives rise to the nonmonotonic thermal conductivity. A similar occupation dependence and spectral redistribution are observed for Ag-embedded g-C3N4. These results identify competing phonon contributions as the microscopic origin of nonmonotonic thermal transport in metal-embedded g-C3N4 and suggest that occupation of intrinsic cavities provides a route to redistributing phonon transport in porous crystalline materials.

items.title: Comparative qualification of advanced plasma-facing materials for fusion pilot plants through public- and private-sector experiments in DIII-D
items.summary: A coordinated DIII-D campaign involving four private fusion developers and 12 participating institutions comparatively assessed 44 advanced plasma-facing materials, including the first DIII-D divertor exposure of neutron-irradiated W, to support fusion pilot plant wall and divertor material qualification. Samples were exposed using the Divertor Materials Evaluation System (DiMES) under Ohmic, L-mode, and H-mode conditions with edge-localized modes, at 0.2-2.5 MW m$^{-2}$ on flush geometries and 10-15 MW m$^{-2}$ on 10$^\circ$ angled geometries. Engineered tungsten architectures retained integrity; long-fiber Wf/W showed the clearest crack-arrest behavior. W-Re and K-doped W showed near-ITER-W-like responses, while additively manufactured W-Ta showed heat-flux-sensitive mass losses of 0.64 mg for the flat sample and 2.19-2.87 mg for angled samples. After irradiation to 0.3 dpa at 550$^\circ$C, neutron-irradiated ITER-grade W retained 2.8 times more deuterium than pristine W, while TiB$2$ showed the lowest D$2$ release in the Ohmic set. VTaHfMo was the most stable refractory multi-principal-element alloy. NbC and (Nb${0.5}$Ta${0.5}$)C retained integrity with 0.02-0.03 mg mass loss, whereas ZrC lost 7 mg. CVD SiC retained macroscopic integrity but exhibited an effective Si erosion yield of 0.5, about 5-10 times above prior DIII-D trends. Renewable boron pebble rods underwent plasma-driven recession; 13% of released boron was ionized near the outer strike point and up to 50% was recovered locally. Initial in-situ Cr gross-erosion measurements yielded effective erosion yields of order $10^{-2}$. Together, these results provide cross-material benchmarks for fusion pilot plant down-selection and future AI/ML-assisted plasma-facing-material development.

items.title: Resolving the Gibbs Paradox through Local Free Space and Collision Potential
items.summary: The Gibbs paradox is conventionally resolved by invoking the indistinguishability of identical particles and the associated $N!$ correction, while the standard entropy of mixing remains independent of molecular properties. Here, we develop a classical framework that does not rely on quantum indistinguishability. We treat molecules initially occupying different spatial regions as distinguishable and describe the accessible volume of each molecule by its instantaneous local free space. We further account for the non-negligible time-averaged potential energy associated with molecular collisions and rederive the entropy increment of gas mixing within the canonical ensemble. The resulting expression depends explicitly on molecular properties, including molecular mass, effective radius, and characteristic collision time, and therefore varies among different gases while yielding zero entropy increment for identical gases naturally. This framework provides a novel classical resolution of the Gibbs paradox by connecting the entropy of mixing to molecular properties rather than to an additional quantum assumption or some new conceptual explanation.

items.title: Pseudo-Altermagnetism in Non-Hermitian Systems
items.summary: Altermagnetism has attracted growing attention, and its analogs have been actively explored across classical platforms. Here, we introduce pseudo-altermagnetism in non-Hermitian systems, where balanced gain and loss plays the role of the altermagnetic spin, and the opposite gain and loss sublattices are related by an antiunitary symmetry $O$ with $O\bm k\neq \bm k$ for generic momentum $\bm k$. Using a two-dimensional non-Hermitian system with $O=C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$ symmetry as a representative example, we find that pseudo-altermagnetism not only leads to a momentum-dependent gain and loss distribution analogous to the momentum-dependent spin splitting of altermagnets, but also exhibits intrinsic non-Hermitian properties. The bands of $C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$-invariant non-Hermitian systems are either isolated or paired by $C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$, and both cases are guaranteed to host movable but unremovable nodal structures, characterized by the zeros of two distinct quantities. An isolated band exhibits two movable but unremovable Hermitian spectral lines, whose generic points are not invariant under $C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$, in sharp contrast to the conventional Hermitian spectra enforced only at the fixed points of an antiunitary symmetry. The paired bands, in turn, feature a movable but unremovable nodal network formed by the union of real-part and imaginary-part degeneracy lines, whose intersections are generally exceptional points. We further demonstrate these findings in a non-Hermitian photonic crystal. Our results establish a symmetry-based bridge between non-Hermitian physics and altermagnetism, and provide novel mechanisms of Hermitian spectra beyond $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry.

items.title: The Sustainability Paradox of Biodegradable Packaging Through a Life Cycle Perspective on Chitosan Based Food Packaging
items.summary: Chitosan-based packaging systems are being studied as alternatives to traditional food packaging made from petroleum sources. The research that has been carried out so far has mostly focused on analyzing their material properties, formulation strategies, or biodegradable behavior. However, as a result, there is a gap left in understanding how the upstream impacts affect the functional advantages of food packaging and the end-of-life results of the formulation process. This review evaluates what trade-offs exist as well as what factors affect the sustainability of chitosan-based packages. Beginning with chitin extraction from crustacean waste, key processing steps, including demineralization, deproteinization, and nanoparticle synthesis, are assessed in terms of chemical intensity, energy demand, and associated emissions. Manufacturing routes, including solvent-based and green synthesis approaches, are compared with those of conventional plastics to identify relative environmental burdens. The use phase is analyzed with respect to antimicrobial functionality, shelf life extension, and potential reductions in food waste. End-of-life pathways, including biodegradation and composting, are evaluated alongside uncertainties related to degradation behavior and nanoparticle fate. The review takes into account life-cycle issues and offers a scientifically based viewpoint on how to differentiate between packaging applications whose environmental benefits can be determined and those whose ecological footprint, lack of functionality, and uncertainty regarding disposal make it impossible to assess sustainability.

items.title: High-Accuracy Neural-Network Quantum States via Randomized Real-Time Dynamics
items.summary: Neural-network quantum states (NQSs) exhibit a disparity in converging to the ground state during energy minimization: while the energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, other observables converge only linearly, which limits the accuracy of physical predictions. Here we show how to close this gap by introducing a new algorithm that improves the accuracy of NQSs. Our method, termed dynamical averaging, estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real-time. Using insights from quantum information, we prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground state observables, thus matching the fast convergence of the energy. Importantly, this improved accuracy requires neither further energy minimization nor increased model complexity, but rather exploits the effect of randomization on quantum states. We demonstrate dynamical averaging on non-integrable spin models, where it accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.

items.title: Mixed-state Phases from Higher-order SSPTs with Kramers-Wannier Symmetry
items.summary: Mixed-state phases have recently attracted significant attention as a generalization beyond their pure-state counterparts. Prominent examples include mixed-state symmetry-protected topological (mSPT) phases and the strong-to-weak symmetry breaking (SWSSB) phases. It has been shown recently that mSPT phases admit a holographic dual description in terms of higher-order subsystem SPT phases. In this work, we investigate the mixed-state phases obtained by tracing out the bulk degrees of freedom of higher-order subsystem SPT phases protected by non-invertible symmetries. We find that the resulting mixed-states exhibit the coexistence of the symmetry-protected topological order and SWSSB. We also use the interface as a probe to characterize the mixed-state phases, and specifically, when there is no local modification to preserve the symmetries across the interface, the two sides of the interface are in distinct phases.

items.title: Pyroelectric Harvesting from Steady Heat Sources via Active Piezoelectric Thermal Switching
items.summary: This study demonstrates pyroelectric energy harvesting from a steady heat source using active piezoelectric thermal switching in a PZT/Si bimorph cantilever. The same PZT layer serves as both the mechanical actuator and the pyroelectric energy-conversion element. Dual output electrodes enable separation of the pyroelectric and piezoelectric signals. Pyroelectric energy harvesting is experimentally demonstrated at frequencies up to 110 Hz and temperature differences as small as 5 K. Comparison with the response predicted from the independently measured pyroelectric coefficient, together with transient thermal simulations, identifies dynamic interfacial heat transfer as a key limitation to high-frequency operation. This work demonstrates a compact MEMS approach for higher-frequency pyroelectric energy harvesting from low-grade steady heat sources.

items.title: Scaling Density Functional Theory with Gaussian Splatting
items.summary: Density functional theory (DFT) strikes a practical balance between accuracy and computational cost in many problems of computational chemistry and materials science. However, many DFT calculations are limited by fixed atom-centered basis sets, which dictate how accuracy and cost scale with system size. We propose Gaussian Splatting for Density Functional Theory (GS-DFT), which represents molecular orbitals as a cloud of Gaussians whose positions, shapes, and mixing coefficients are optimized jointly by gradient descent to minimize the energy without training data. Conceptually, GS-DFT is 3D Gaussian splatting with the renderer replaced by quantum mechanics. We introduce two key solver components: adaptive density fitting with screening for efficient evaluation of two-electron integrals, and a regularized differentiable orthogonalization of the molecular orbitals. Empirically, the optimized basis reaches the accuracy of the largest conventional basis sets with a fraction of the parameters, converging systematically in energy, density, and nuclear forces. At equal parameter count, it captures the stretched-bond and anion physics that fixed bases only recover with specialized basis augmentation. The resulting solver exhibits quadratic peak memory scaling in the cloud size, allowing us to simulate systems of up to 2,742 atoms (10,406 electrons) without any modifications at triple-zeta scale using a single four-GPU node.

items.title: Stationary covariance spectra of discrete-time non-normal random recurrent dynamics
items.summary: Principal component analysis is widely used to characterize structure in the dynamics of recurrent neural networks. For stationary noise-driven dynamics, the distribution of variance among the principal components is determined by the spectrum of the stationary covariance matrix. While the spectral properties of this matrix are well-understood for linear networks with normal synaptic weight matrices, our understanding of the stationary covariance spectrum for random non-normal dynamics remains incomplete. In this note, we use a free-probability approach to show almost-sure convergence of the stationary covariance spectrum of discrete-time dynamics with random non-normal Gaussian weights, and derive a closed functional equation characterizing its distribution. This characterization allows us to analyze the behavior of tail eigenvalues in the critical regime: they decay with the inverse-square of their rank. In contrast, applying the same approach to the analogous continuous-time dynamics leads to an infinite hierarchy of Schwinger-Dyson equations, rather than a closed scalar equation.

items.title: Unveiling the Complex high-pressure phases of Sodium at the Melting Curve Minimum via Data-Drive Crystal Structure Prediction
items.summary: Sodium exhibits a remarkable concentration of complex crystalline phases near its melting-curve minimum, yet the atomic arrangements of several experimentally observed phases remain unresolved. Here, we combine CALYPSO crystal structure prediction with Deep Potential models developed through concurrent learning to explore this structural landscape. Searches over more than 1.6 million configurations recover the previously reported $I4/m$ structure of $tI50$ and identify candidate atomic arrangements for $oC120$ and $aP90$, together with three additional low-enthalpy structures, $tI52$, $oP72$, and $oP92$. The proposed candidates reproduce key features of the experimentally indexed cell geometries. First-principles enthalpy calculations, Gibbs free-energy comparisons, and solid--liquid coexistence simulations reveal close competition among these structures and established sodium phases. Near the calculated reference melting minimum, $tI50$ is favored over $cI16$ and $oP8$, whereas $oC120$ and $aP90$ remain closely competitive, with their relative stability sensitive to model accuracy. These results provide testable structural models for unresolved experimental phases and reveal multiple closely competing low-enthalpy configurations near sodium's melting minimum

items.title: Sondheimer oscillations in Weyl semimetal films
items.summary: In conducting films subject to an out-of-plane magnetic field, electron motion between the surfaces gives rise to conductance oscillations periodic in magnetic field, known as Sondheimer oscillations. While this size effect has been investigated in conventional metals, its dependence on the Berry curvature of topological materials remains less explored. In this work, we extend the semiclassical Boltzmann description of Sondheimer oscillations to type-I Weyl semimetal films. We account for the Berry curvature, the orbital magnetic moment and the effect of the Zeeman coupling on the Fermi wavevector and the electronic group velocity. The Berry curvature and the orbital magnetic moment generate a beating pattern and chirping in the Sondheimer oscillations. In the thick-film and thin-film regimes, we provide analytical expressions for the longitudinal conductivity, which highlight the interplay between electronic band topology and boundary-scattering in magnetotransport.

items.title: Electric polarizabilities with phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo
items.summary: While projector quantum Monte Carlo methods are known for producing accurate ground-state energies, the prediction of other properties that encode the electronic response to applied electric and magnetic fields has historically been challenging. In this work we demonstrate that the electric (static) polarizability tensor, which is formally a second-derivative of the energy with respect to electric fields, can be efficiently computed with phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo using a correlated sampling finite-difference strategy. With simple Hartree-Fock trial wave functions, we investigate a series of small molecules (some of which are difficult for approximate density functionals), polyacenes of increasing size, and ferrocene as a representative organometallic complex. The methodology is scalable to relatively large molecules involving thousands of basis functions, and with appropriate trial wave functions remains robust for strongly correlated electronic states, as we show for the stretched dinitrogen molecule. This work opens the door to the computation of a host of other second-order molecular properties with auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo, which will inform the ongoing search for optimal trial wave functions and extend benchmark-quality training data sets for the refinement of semi-empirical and machine learning models for quantum chemistry and molecular simulation.

items.title: Molecular regulation and recurrent evolution of fungal bet-hedging conidiation
items.summary: Abstract Bet-hedging (BH) mitigates risk in fluctuating environments by promoting phenotypic diversity within a single genotype. Fungi exhibit remarkable phenotypic plasticity, such as conidiation polymorphism. Here, we show that entomopathogenic Metarhizium species produce either monomorphic or dimorphic conidia, which exhibit marked size variation to support different BH strategies. The large cylindrical and small ovoid conidia produced by the same species possess complementary advantages that facilitate adaptation to different conditions. Large conidia are heavily pigmented, ultraviolet-resistant, and highly virulent, whereas small conidia, produced either on separate phialides or atop large ones, germinate faster and resist bacteria better. These complementary traits represent a classic, yet previously unsuspected, diversified BH strategy. Mechanistic analysis revealed distinct gene expression patterns between morphotypes, leading to the identification of a transcription factor and a lipid-droplet surface protein that play key roles in governing dimorphic conidiation and pigmentation. Phylogenomic reconstruction revealed that later-diverging species reverted to an ancestral, monomorphic medium-spore state, indicating a recurrence of the conservative BH strategy. Pairwise experimental evolution confirmed that monomorphic populations have a fitness advantage under fluctuating ultraviolet irradiation. Our findings establish the BH mechanism in conidiation and reveal evolutionary experimentation with reversion across fungal speciation.

items.title: Nanocatalytic modulation of thrombin-ferroptosis axis for efficient intervention of ischemic stroke
items.summary: Abstract Ischemic stroke represents a leading cause of global mortality. Current therapeutic strategies, including recombinant tissue plasminogen activator and mechanical thrombectomy, are constrained by suboptimal recanalization, high recurrence rates, and reperfusion injury. In this work, we initially identified elevated intrathrombotic thrombin as a critical mediator of fibrinolytic resistance and a driver of ferroptosis-related neuronal injury following stroke. To specifically target this thrombin dysregulation, we designed ultrasmall tungsten-based polyoxometalate (W-POM) nanodots capable of penetrating the blood-brain barrier. In addition to their specific reactive oxygen species-scavenging capability, W-POM nanodots primarily modulate thrombin activity and attenuate its pathological signaling. In both thrombin-induced and ischemia-reperfusion injury models, W-POM nanodots significantly improve neurological outcomes by directly suppressing thrombin activity and inhibiting thrombin-driven ferroptosis. Furthermore, W-POM nanodots remodel the thrombotic microenvironment and reduce neuroinflammation, thereby conferring robust neuroprotection. This study highlights the thrombin-ferroptosis pathway as a key mechanistic axis in stroke and introduces a nanotherapeutic platform for targeted thrombin modulation in ischemic stroke therapy.

items.title: Nucleophile–electrophile chemistry produces a stable interphase for long-Life anode-Less lithium metal batteries
items.summary: Abstract Anode-less lithium (Li) metal batteries (ALLMBs) represent the optimal cell architecture for maximizing energy density, yet their practical viability is severely hindered by poor cycling life. This limitation stems from the unstable solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI), which drives continuous parasitic reactions with Li metal and induces severe interfacial degradation. Here we report a nucleophile–electrophile bridging strategy to construct a robust, passivating SEI that enables long-term stable cycling of ALLMBs. By leveraging a nucleophilic substitution mechanism, electron-rich organic species derived from the solvent, acting as nucleophiles, are covalently bridged by electron-deficient, boron-centred electrophiles derived from the anion. This molecular-level integration overcomes the inherent fragility of the SEI organic phase, generating mechanically robust oligoborates that resist interfacial degradation, along with lithium fluoride (LiF) nanocrystals nucleated in-situ to facilitate rapid Li + transport. The resulting oligoborate–LiF hybrid SEI enables highly reversible Li plating/stripping and remarkably extends the ALLMB cycling life by 12-fold, maintaining 80% capacity over 300 cycles. The superior cyclability is maintained even under stringent practical conditions (high cathode loading, lean electrolyte supply, and pouch-cell operation). This work establishes a fundamentally new paradigm in interphase engineering, paving the way for high-energy, reliable ALLMBs.

items.title: Room temperature giant in-plane anomalous Hall effect in TbMn6Sn6
items.summary: Abstract The anomalous Hall effect is the transverse voltage response in the presence of out-of-plane magnetization or non-zero Berry curvature, which, traditionally, is modulated by an out-of-plane magnetic field. Here we demonstrate a giant in-plane anomalous Hall effect (AHE) induced by coplanar magnetic fields in the quantum magnet TbMn 6 Sn 6 at room temperature. The very large Hall conductivity arises in response to an applied in-plane magnetic field and results from the tilting of the ferrimagnetic axis of the Mn and Tb moments to the out of plane direction. With the in-plane magnetic field aligning the ferrimagnetic axis, the Berry curvature induced giant anomalous Hall effect is observed. Further, we show that the in-plane field induced AHE is more pronounced below the temperature induced spin reorientation, showing a 2π periodicity in angular dependent measurements. Unlike the in-plane Hall effect previously observed primarily at low temperatures, the AHE we observe here represents the largest room-temperature response reported in a single material. Our results reveal strong coupling between an in-plane magnetic field and out-of-plane Berry curvature, enabling new opportunities to engineer spintronic and quantum device responses at practical operating temperatures.

items.title: Solar assisted lithium recovery from brines: challenges and opportunities for integrated system
items.summary: Abstract The rapid projected increases in demand for batteries over the upcoming decades requires a large expansion of lithium production capacity. While hard rock mining currently dominates the worldwide production, brines hold over 60% of global lithium reserves. Lithium production from brines is hampered by low lithium concentrations and high concentrations of other interfering ions such as magnesium. This review comprehensively analyzes integrated solar evaporation methods for capturing the lithium in brines. By firstly reviewing the conventional solar evaporation-chemical precipitation method, a currently commercialized technique, we identify several key challenges, including long timescales, large environmental impacts, and issues capturing lithium in some brine chemistries which prevents it from being applied in more places. A promising strategy to address these challenges is integrating interfacial solar evaporation with adsorption materials. This integration presents several advantages, such as producing both high evaporation and lithium adsorption rates and separating lithium from interfering ions. However, a key issue that needs careful evaluation is scaling taking place on the evaporative surface over time, which can cause significant drops in evaporative flux, thereby lowering the effectiveness of this integrated method. Several anti-scaling technologies have been reported, among which integrated membrane and solar evaporation systems demonstrate excellent potential in maintaining long-term performance of high evaporation and lithium capture rates. Ultimately, integrating interfacial solar evaporation with adsorption/membrane processes has the potential to provide a versatile and sustainable method for capturing lithium from brines with complex compositions.

items.title: Photothermal-driven CO2 hydrogenation to methanol on an integrated Au–MoS2–TiO2 catalyst
items.summary: Abstract Light-driven CO 2 hydrogenation to methanol is constrained by insufficient broadband light utilization and inefficient CO 2 activation. Herein, we achieve highly efficient photothermal hydrogenation of CO 2 to methanol on an integrated Au–MoS 2 –TiO 2 catalyst, in which MoS 2 is anchored on TiO 2 to form an intimate interface, and Au nanoparticles (NPs) are deposited on MoS 2 –TiO 2 . We demonstrate that the MoS 2 –TiO 2 interface induces the formation of few-layered MoS 2 and transfers electrons from TiO 2 to MoS 2 . MoS 2 serves as the primary active phase for CO 2 hydrogenation, while Au NPs enhance photo-to-heat conversion via the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) effect, thereby collectively facilitating CO 2 activation under mild reaction conditions. Under photothermal conditions at 120°C in a continuous-flow reactor, the catalyst achieves 13.4% CO 2 conversion with 84.7% methanol selectivity, and maintains stable performance over 400 hours without observable deactivation, underscoring it among the most competitive photothermal catalysts for CO 2 hydrogenation to methanol.
